# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies like Bullet Train and The Nice Guys — funny, violent, fast-paced crime comedies with great lead chemistry

**Score:** 76
**Body:** Looking for feature films with a similar tone to these two:

* **Bullet Train** (2022) — stylized action, ensemble of quirky hitmen, dark comedy, colorful neon visuals, constant momentum
* **The Nice Guys** (2016) — mismatched buddy duo, noir mystery, slapstick violence, sharp banter, 70s LA setting

**What I'm specifically looking for:**

* Crime or hitman underworld setting
* Comedy that coexists with real violence (not parody, not full comedy)
* Strong lead chemistry / buddy dynamic
* Fast pacing with a plot that keeps moving
* Stylish direction — neon, retro, or heightened aesthetic

**What I'm NOT looking for:**

* Grim, self-serious crime dramas (no Se7en, No Country for Old Men, etc.)
* Straight-up spoofs or parodies
* Slow-burn character studies

I've already seen and enjoyed: Kiss Kiss Bang Bang, Snatch, Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, Hot Fuzz, The Gentlemen.

## 5. What is a good movie to show high school seniors about bad things happening to good people?

**Score:** 33
**Body:** I teach a Theology class at a Catholic High Shcool and we're exploring the book of Job. We're tackling subjects like the problem of evil, why bad things happen to good people, and abandonment. 

I was thinking of showing them A Serious Man. I watched it in college and have always loved it since (plus it's literally a modern retelling of the story of Job), but I wanted to see what else was out there that might be able to get the same effect. I'm worried that A Serious Man might be too mature for them or might go over their heads.

All of my students are at least 17 so rating isn't an issue. Thank you all in advance!

I want to recommend The Fisher King (1991) but there’s a full frontal nudity scene with Robin Williams. So good otherwise, maybe save this one for yourself if you haven’t seen it or find a censored version

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. What movie did you completely misunderstand when you were younger?

**Score:** 2047
**Body:** For me, it might be 500 Days of Summer…  
When I was younger, I saw Tom as the hopeless romantic and Summer as the person who broke his heart.  
Watching it again years later, I started seeing it differently. Tom seems to fall in love not only with Summer, but with the version of their relationship he has created in his head.  
Summer was pretty clear about what she wanted, while Tom kept hoping the relationship would eventually become something else,,,  
did Summer actually break Tom’s heart, or did Tom break his own heart by expecting her to become the person he wanted her to be?  
Has a movie ever completely changed meaning for you as you got older?

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. A Goofy Movie. As a kid you see things from Max’s point of view but as an adult you see things from Goofy’s point of view
  - As a kid you think the music is great. As an adult you appreciate how hard Tevin Campbell worked to deliver top tier music.
    - Tevin Campbell really should have had a big break after this. He should be a household name (outside my house) 
  - As an adult, Goofy should have sat Max down and asked for his version of events. 

Max wasn’t a problem child. He wasn’t a delinquent. The kid’s biggest issue was getting a girl he liked to notice him. 

So Goofy deciding that Max is at risk of being part of a chain gang based on a single phone call from the principal - who Goofy doesn’t appear to have met at all, which further indicates that Max wasn’t really an issue and the principal was being a tool - is very out of left field. 

I bet he’d have been so supportive and proud if he’d known his 14-15 year old basically did a live solo performance and Michael Jackson’d in front of the whole school. He would rave about how his little Maxie was a hopeless romantic just like him, and they’d probably even have a touching story about some grand romantic gesture Goofy did for Max’s mother when they were dating. 
    - well shucks

![gif](giphy|XUYS8qIqOt2KOBl3N5)


2. Hook. As a grownup with kids I totally get Peter in a way I didn't as a kid. 

The Sandlot. Way different when you are in the spring of life vs. an adult.  

3. Scrooged, in a really weird way. When he was floating outside the young boys house looking in the window, I thought he was viewing his childhood. The family was Black. I therefore thought that we all changed skin colors throughout life, and therefore concluded I would be a Black man when I grew up. I was 4 or 5.
  - “I was born a poor black child…”
4. Starship troopers.

When I saw that movie as a kid, I thought it was a stupid hoo-rah American war movie. The movie completely lacks nuance and I remember thinking that you really got to be dumb to not be able to see through the shitty propaganda. To me it was a movie made for stupid American teenagers to encourage them to join the military.

Didn't realize until a rewatch in adulthood that that's exactly the point, it was made to be very obvious satire. The parallels to Nazi Germany with the ubermensch protagonist are so obvious on a rewatch, even the uniforms match.
5. The Little Mermaid

As a kid I thought King Triton was an overprotective dad who was mean to Ariel.

Now as a dad, I’m watching it saying King Triton should be angry at Ariel.

## 3. The characters in Prometheus (2012) are so out of character

**Score:** 477
**Body:** I gave this movie a second try after a long time, and I don't think it gets any better the second time around.

These supposed "smart" people cannot be more unbelievable. Uff, I mean, the supposed "biologist" literally sticks his face to an unknown, weird-looking snake that looks like something straight out of All Tomorrows. He literally freaked out at the mere idea that there were aliens there, but is okay with this one and treats it like a puppy? Okay.

The geologist getting lost on his own map scan, great. He even mocks the protagonist in the early sequence of the movie. What do you mean? Don't you know what you're there for?

And they voluntarily took off their respirators inside an unknown alien structure just because the atmosphere was breathable. There could literally be something in there that we don't know about. Wonderful.

Literally, what's the point of writing them in all these highly specialized roles when you can't really make their behavior believable? Just make them some random dudes from San Francisco and it would be more believable.

The realism mixed with the sci fi is what makes Alien such a good film. Its a believable world. Idk if Scott just had different priorities this time around or if he just couldnt be arsed.
6. IIRC, the original idea was that they weren't the best and brightest, they were marginally-qualified fuck-ups willing to go at the drop of a hat, in extreme secrecy, for a big payday. If that sub-plot had made it into the final draft, the movie would have made so much more sense.

## 4. The Sopranos or The Wire? Which show do you think is the better show overall?

**Score:** 300
**Body:** Both are widely considered among the greatest TV shows ever made, and they’re constantly compared even though they’re doing pretty different things.  
*The Sopranos* is a dark comedy/crime drama built around Tony Soprano: a mob boss trying to balance crime, family, marriage, kids, therapy and friendships. The mafia stuff is obviously central, but so is all the everyday dysfunction. At times, it almost feels like a twisted crime family sitcom.

*The Wire* is a much broader, more straight up drama with no single main character. It starts with Baltimore’s drug trade and police department, then expands into the schools, politics, docks and media. Instead of focusing mainly on one person, it looks at how different institutions work and how they shape the lives of the people stuck inside them.

Basically, *The Sopranos* is more intimate, character driven and personal, while *The Wire* is broader, more systemic and focused on the bigger picture.  
If you could only keep one, which one is the better show overall, *The Sopranos* or *The Wire*?

3. The Wire was probably a better show...but I was often not in the mood to watch The Wire, and rarely not in the mood to watch The Sopranos.
  - Whenever this conversation takes place, I always default to this idea: The Wire is huge in scope, it’s about society writ large and all the different pieces that make it up and their dysfunction. The erosion of America viewed from all angles, from the hood to the mayor’s office to the blue-collar union workers and media.

Meanwhile, the Sopranos is just an incredibly well written show about a few people and their fucked up lives. It’s much more personal.

Both shows of course, tell big stories and small stories, explore large themes and very personal ones. But overall, the wire is massive and analytical in scope, the Sopranos is a personal exploration of a group of very well written people.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. What are some of the Best Actors with Small Filmographies?

**Score:** 36
**Body:** Question, What do you think are the best actors that have the smallest filmographies.

I'm asking this because I decided to look up Paul Muni and Robert Donat. Great Actors, but looking at their filmographies, I'm just like, "That's All, They really did not do a lot of films". Paul Muni did a total of 23 films and Donat did 19 films.

Another actor is Paul Scofield. Scofield is just a great actor and every time he appears in a film, he elevates them (A Man For All Seasons, Quiz Show, The Crucible), but he only did only a few films throughout his entire career and I just wish he did more films.

I know there are other reasons as to why. Probably because of theater work or doing other things in life. But it's just a shame when an actor has a small filmography, because you're left wanting more from them.

All in All, What do you think are the best actors that have the smallest filmographies.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. John Cazale starred in 7 films and 5 of those were some of the most revered films of all time: The Godfather, The Conversation, The Godfather Part II, Dog Day Afternoon and The Deer Hunter.
  - Really 5 films. The other two was a tv series and a short film. He’s the GOAT of this conversation.
    - Him and James Dean are pretty much the tragic kings of this.
    - AND he was in love with Meryl Streep, possibly the greatest actress of all time. Cazale knew how to pick his roles and his partners, the man was a legend
  - Every one got a Best Picture nomination.
  - He died at just 42 years old from lung cancer. His partner at the time was Meryl Streep who stood by him all through his sickness and treatments until he passed. It’s such a sad story but also really beautiful knowing how devoted she was to him in his final days.
2. James Dean is on this Mount Rushmore for sure. Only had a 5 year run and maybe only was a massive superstar for 2-3 of those, and still defines a certain level of moviestar coolness to this day.

You almost forget he was a real actor and not just a symbol of "gone too soon," but goddam he had IT.
3. There are lot of examples of great actors that just failed on breaking through into being in high demand. The example that jumps out in my mind is https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin\_Joston. 

He was really good in Assault on Precinct 13, and had some success with other John Carpenter films, but for some reason that success never translated into other roles. 
4. Anton Yelchin could have gone so far. Just look at Green Room.

It would be interesting to do a sub-category here of people who fit this description who did NOT tragically die in their prime.
  - 100% Anton Yelchin. He was so so good. I feel like he could have balanced out those few years after he passed of all these smaller (as in less leading-man bulky type) restless guy kind of roles going right to Timothee Chalamet, with his own softer, less intense and more thoughtful kind of energy. His supporting role in Only Lovers Left Alive was also so fun. He just seemed so grounded, Green Room let him show such a range from the tense scenes to the ending. RIP.

## 2. Cesare from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari got me thinking about how sometimes we know absolutely nothing about characters who are central to the story.

**Score:** 13
**Body:** We only ever see him as a killer, even though we know he’s under Caligari’s control. But then it suddenly occurred to me… who is he, and what is he actually like outside of his trance? There’s an entirely different person hidden in the shadows.

Or, for a slightly stranger example, Leatherface’s mask in the original *Texas Chainsaw Massacre*. Whose face is that? We’re looking at this person throughout the entire movie, yet we never really stop to think about who we’re actually looking at or what happened to them!

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. There’s a term for what you have mentioned: narrative erasure. It occurs when a story focuses so intensely on what a character *does* that *who* they are (or used to be) is relegated almost entirely in the shadows.

But why is it common mostly in the horror genre, one might ask.   
  
Reason being, it creates a sense of dread that is unique. A dread that dawns upon us slowly as we realize that *who* we are watching (in the context of the two examples you provided) were once human; and has now been stripped of their identity only to be weaponized to function as an object/tool/prop.   
  
This also creates an uncanny void, in the sense that when we watch on screen a human face/body, we are wired to expect a human mind behind it. But when we are faced with an absence (or in some cases a tabula rasa) it creates an unsettling vacuum.

There are several other equally famous examples of this in cinema, including Alex Murphy in *RoboCop* (1987), the pod people in *Invasion of the Body Snatchers* (1978); and even non-human instances, like the Necronomicon in *The Evil Dead* (yes, it’s a book but every inch of its leather cover was once part of a human being).
2. Maybe this is not exactly the same thing, but I'm always interested in the lives of minor characters. Two works come to mind that follow minor "stock" characters, making them the protagoists--Rosencrantz and Gildenstern are Dead and Pulp Fiction. 

## 3. Ashes and Diamonds (1958 dir. Andrzej Wajda)

**Score:** 8
**Body:** I've tried watching this film a few times now, but I've never made it past the first 20 minutes or thereabouts because I'm so confused by everything. Basically, I don't understand why, as Polish resistance fighters, Maciek and Andrzej have been asked to kill this man who is presumably somewhat closely aligned with them politically, seeing as he's not a collaborator with the Nazis. Then there's the Major, who appears to have a portrait of a Nazi officer (?) hanging on his wall despite being the director of a resistance cell - did he see which way the wind was blowing and jump ship before the resistance could take him out? Also, he says something to Andrzej along the lines of, "Once all this is over you're likely to end up in prison" - why would this be the case for someone who's been fighting in the resistance?

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. "...why would this be the case for someone who's been fighting in the resistance?"

Because the was a divide in the Polish resistance movement. There were nationalist partisans who wanted an independent Poland and there were Marxist-Leninist resistance fighters who wanted to bring Poland into the orbit of the USSR.

Stalin wanted the Polish nationalist partisans purged. The Red Army allowed the Germans to destroy Warsaw during the '44 uprising in order to crush this nationalist resistance movement. 

See also the Katyn massacre. 
2. It's been over a decade since I last saw the movie, so I can't speak to all the specific details, but the main source of your confusion is the timeline. The movie doesn't take place during WWII; it's set shortly after. Maciek used to be in the Home Army (the armed wing of the Polish Underground State), but after its dissolution he joined the anti-communist underground.

## 4. How major are the differences between the different versions of Napoleon (1927) and is there one that is seen as the "definitive" one to watch?

1. I can't tell you about specific differences, because I've only seen the 5.5hr Brownlow 2004 cut w/ Carl Davis score; I was fortunate enough to catch an incredibly rare screening at Film Forum last year and it was great.

so much of the film was lost for so long (including the "Apollo cut"), that anything you can watch now will be a reconstruction.  the 4hr Coppola cut is missing much footage that has been discovered in the years since. the 7hr Mourier cut has only been screened once, in 2024 with three projectors and an orchestra, and no one knows when it might be shown again.

so until it does, the Brownlow cut, which was a comprehensive scholarly attempt to recreate the "Apollo cut" as best as possible with the available footage, is your best bet. last year's Blu-ray box set is sold out, but if you search archive.org you'll find someone has ripped and uploaded it.

I think the only reason to watch the Coppola version would be if 
you are a huge enough fan of his to be curious to hear his father's score. otherwise you're seeing something further away from the original intent.

## 5. What makes a film feel long?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I rewatched Anatomy of a murder yesterday. Before watching i honestly didnt remember it was almost 3 hours and after finishing it I realized why i didnt remember its lenght. It is a really entertaining movie. In paper it shouldnt be as entertaining as it is. Most of the movie is basically one trial in one location. There arent any action, there is no music in most of the movie, and there is a lot of fluff that could be cut down and it would be probably a better movie. But the movie is genuinely very entertaining and i really couldn´t feel the lenght. 

Now i want to compare it to High and Low. High and Low is an amazing movie and also very entertaining but watching the movie feels very long. It is feels a lot more longer than anatomy of a murder being 20 minutes shorter. I dont want to shitalk the movie because it is an amazing movie and of course some people will have a different reaction watching these two movies. But why i felt that way?

High and Low is a police procedural. It is very different to Anatomy of a murder but it has a lot of similarities. Both of them are about a crime, both of them are black and white, both of them are a social commentaries. But I think there are some reasons why high and low feels longer. High and low, as most Kurosawa films are, is about one thing and one thing only. Every scene is moving the plot and they are all interesting but you are always thinking about this one crime. The progression is fairly linear and there arent a lot of twist and turns. The police want to catch this criminal and every scene is a natural progression of that. the clues and the methods are very interesting but one is waiting that they catch it. The police dont have a strong personality so there isnt that counterbalance to add variaty. Every scene is about one thing and one thing only.  

While anatomy of a murder it is about a crime being a trial every examination allows to have more variety. Every new witness adds a new perspective and something new that the audience must ponder about. And basically every trial scene is a dramatic scene with the witness being the dramatic center and the bonus of seeing the defence and prosecucion arguing about the new information. Also even if it has a kinda simple plot the progression isnt as linear and there are some twist that surprises the audience. And having a larger cast and more charismatic characters it can break the monotony of the trial having more relaxing scenes and some humour (as bad as the humour is in the movie).

Again before i end this post i just wanted to say that I considere High and Low a better movie overall. I just wanted to ponder what makes the movie feel so short being so long at least to me.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. > There arent any action, there is no music in most of the movie

Some of the most boring movies are nonstop action and music.

It's all about emotional engagement. It's why 10 minutes playing a video game might seem short, but 10 minutes waiting in line at the grocery store is incredibly frustrating.

Black and white doesn't matter, books are black and white, and some are engaging while others are dry. 

Also humans are curious so we love a mystery and we're engaged while clues are discovered, we sit to attention for the next clue.
2. Pacing, most heavily influenced by editing. This can make shorter movies feel longer and vice versa. I think you're focusing too much on plot. Plot is malleable, it conforms to the writing and the editing. 

A recent example for me is The Odyssey - despite being 3 hours long, it felt incredibly rushed because it was edited into a choppy mess...
3. Laughing Sinners (1931) made me think about this. The film is only 72 minutes long but I felt it dragging somehow. The best reason I could pinpoint is that the characters and plot were not interesting. 
4. To me it's all about rhythm, like for instance Drive My Car is by any account a fairly slow-paced 3 hour film that somehow still glides by beautifully because it's filled with little ebbs and flows of narrative and character that give it a real pulse. Apparently Martin Scorsese taps his hand while watching scenes he's directing because he always has pacing on his mind and it explains why the likes of Goodfellas is a 2.5 hour movie that somehow feels like it's 90 minutes long too.
5. Oh my gosh, I also rewatched Anatomy of a Murder, and I also had the thought of "that was the fastest two hours and forty minutes of my life."

I think what really does it is the pacing, particularly the rhythm. This might be the most perfectly paced movie of all time, because so much of it is just people delivering dialogue, but it sets up a perfect rhythm of constantly readdressing the events that set the story in motion with increasingly more explicit detail. And of course all of the performances are just brilliant. 
6. The most important factor is execution. A long movie REALLY needs to justify it, ideally by making each scene an engaging watch. All of the long films I enjoy have exceptional cinematography which makes it feel like I’m perusing an art museum even if the film is slow. 

Long films also need to do one of 2 things to keep my attention. They need to escalate / change scenery (2001 does this for me), OR they need to set the slow tone VERY deliberately from the start to hypnotize me a little. Jeanne Dielman and Stalker do this well IMO.

Oppenheimer on the other hand felt pretty exhausting because of its pacing 
  - What makes Stalker not as boring as it is it because every scene as basic as they are it always slowly progressing. It never stops. It has such a great pace it is amazing. I watched it with my mother and she really like it.
7. Yeah, I found myself loosing steam in the last 30 minutes of High and Low but it is EXTRAORDINARY nevertheless. 

Speaking of Kurosawa, Seven Samurai comes first to mind when talking about movies that *feel* long. It’s 3.5 hours but feels even longer… because it’s supposed to. We are supposed to feel the mounting fear and the anxious waiting. It’s brilliant. 

It is fascinating to look at something like Lawrence of Arabia, which is 4 hours by contrast, yet it feels even shorter than Seven Samurai. 

As others have pointed out, it has to do all with the editing and intention. The pacing of Lawrence is brilliantly balanced with action, dialogue, and quiet moments. It’s a perfectly edited 4 hour film imo.

Yeah, Seven Samurai is slower, but it’s a creative choice that really does work well as long as you’re not too sleepy and stoned going into it. 

Fascinating phenomenon 
  - > It’s 3.5 hours but feels even longer… because it’s supposed to. We are supposed to feel the mounting fear and the anxious waiting.

Yep. There are lots of good movies that feel long in a good way. They feel like you've lived an experience with the characters. Older movies were more this way. Tootsie comes to mind as a not-that-long (1hr 50min) light-hearted comic movie, that charts its course so well that by the end you feel you've been there and it's weeks or months later. There's something about the realness of the characters emotions, and the way a movie goes in and out of scenes, that can give you a sense of time passing without making it feel slow. It's rare these days that a movie can do that for me. It was probably rare back in the day as well, we just remember the good ones.
